tagline: Alps, waltzes, and grand old coffeehouses
overview:
Austria is a landlocked country in the heart of Central Europe, slightly smaller than the US state of Maine, where the Alps cover more than half the land. Its capital, Vienna, sits on the Danube River in the flat northeast and was for centuries the seat of one of Europe's most powerful royal families, the Habsburgs. Their palaces, opera houses, and grand cafés still give the city an imperial air. About 9 million people live in Austria, roughly a fifth of them in and around Vienna.

German is the official language, spoken in a distinctive Austrian accent and dialect. Austria is a federal republic of nine states with a parliament and a chancellor who leads the government. It has been officially neutral since 1955 and joined the European Union in 1995. Austrians are known for music, having produced Mozart, Haydn, Schubert, and the Strauss family of waltz composers, and for winter sports, with skiing close to a national religion. Villages of onion-domed churches and flower-decked wooden chalets fill the mountain valleys.
landAndNature: The Alps sweep across western and central Austria, topped by the Grossglockner at nearly 3,800 meters, with the Pasterze glacier at its foot. Hohe Tauern National Park, the largest in the Alps, shelters ibex, marmots, golden eagles, and bearded vultures that were brought back after disappearing. The Krimml Waterfalls tumble about 380 meters in three stages, among the tallest in Europe. In the north the Danube cuts through vineyards and forested hills, while the far east flattens into steppe around Lake Neusiedl, a shallow reed-fringed lake shared with Hungary and crowded with birds. Winters are snowy and cold in the mountains; summers are warm. Beneath the peaks near Werfen lies Eisriesenwelt, the largest ice cave in the world.
peopleAndCulture: Austrian life blends old and new. Vienna's coffeehouses, where a single cup buys hours at a marble table with newspapers, are on UNESCO's cultural heritage list. Favorite foods include Wiener schnitzel, a thin breaded veal or pork cutlet, apple strudel, fluffy shredded pancakes called Kaiserschmarrn, and the chocolate Sachertorte. Every New Year's Day the Vienna Philharmonic plays waltzes to a worldwide television audience, and the winter ball season fills palaces with dancers. Salzburg hosts a famous summer music festival and was the setting for the film The Sound of Music. Austrian skiers have won more Alpine World Cup races than any other nation, and children in mountain villages often ski before they can read. Traditional dirndl dresses and lederhosen appear at festivals.
history: Celts and then Romans settled the region, founding Vindobona, which became Vienna. From 1278 the Habsburg family ruled Austria for more than 600 years, expanding into an empire that stretched across Central Europe and twice fought off Ottoman armies at the gates of Vienna, in 1529 and 1683. The assassination of the Habsburg heir Franz Ferdinand in 1914 triggered World War I, and the empire collapsed in 1918. The small new republic was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938, and Austrian Jews suffered persecution and murder in the Holocaust. After World War II the country was occupied by the Allies until 1955, when it regained independence by promising permanent neutrality. Austria joined the European Union in 1995 and adopted the euro.
funFacts: The snow globe was invented in Vienna in 1900 by a man trying to make a brighter surgical lamp.
The Christmas carol Silent Night was first sung in 1818 in the small Austrian town of Oberndorf.
Vienna's Schönbrunn Zoo opened in 1752 and is the oldest zoo in the world still operating.
PEZ candy was created in Vienna in 1927 as a breath mint for adults; the name comes from Pfefferminz, German for peppermint.
The Eisriesenwelt ice cave stretches for about 42 kilometers, and its ice never fully melts.
